entries.title: The Chateaubriand with Foyot
entries.summary: The thick centre of the beef tenderloin, roasted whole and carved for two, with sauce Foyot, a béarnaise deepened with meat glaze. The cut brings tenderness; the sauce brings the depth the mild meat lacks.
entries.guest: The Chateaubriand serves two: the thick centre of a Creekstone Farms tenderloin, roasted whole, with glazed summer squash and sauce Foyot, a béarnaise made richer with a reduced meat glaze.

paras: A Chateaubriand is the thick centre of the beef tenderloin, the long, slender muscle under the spine that does almost no work. Because it barely moves, it is the tenderest meat on the animal and also the mildest, with little fat running through it. The centre is the even, round stretch between the tapering tail and the knobbly head, so it roasts evenly and carves into neat slices. Cooked whole, it feeds two: a celebration plate, roasted, rested and carved for the table.

Sauce Foyot (fwah-YO) does the other half of the work: béarnaise, the tarragon butter sauce, with glace de viande, meat glaze, whisked in. The glaze, brown stock reduced until thick and syrupy, turns a pale, sharp béarnaise tawny and savoury, which is exactly what the mildest cut lacks. Making the sauce, and the story of its name, belong to Choron and Foyot.

The name honours François-René de Chateaubriand, the French writer and diplomat. Tradition credits his chef, Montmireil, with the dish around 1822; tell it as a story. Butchers define the cut in different ways: in France it is usually a thick steak from the heart of the fillet, the British name for the tenderloin; some older books take it from the head end; and in America it often means the whole centre-cut roast for two.

A Chateaubriand for two weighs roughly 450 to 680 g (16 to 24 oz) trimmed. Strip off the silverskin, the tough, shiny membrane that never softens, and tie the meat at 2.5 cm (1 inch) intervals so it holds an even round. Salt it well, sear it on every side in a hot pan for 6 to 8 minutes until deep brown, then roast it at about 200°C (392°F) for 15 to 25 minutes, checking the centre with a probe thermometer.

Pull it before the finish, because stored heat carries on into the centre as it rests: about 51°C (124°F) for a medium-rare finish near 55°C (131°F). Rest it on a rack, loosely covered, for about 10 minutes; the theory belongs to Roast and baste. Then remove the string and carve across the grain, which in a tenderloin runs the length of the muscle, into slices about 2 cm (3/4 inch) thick. Sauce at the last moment: Foyot is a warm emulsion, and a scorching plate splits it.

One roast comes to one temperature, so doneness is agreed once, with both guests. The ends are always a little more done than the centre, but sending the ends to one guest and the centre to the other is the kitchen's decision, never the server's promise.

A grey band under the crust means too much heat for too long. Done at one end and raw at the other means the meat was not tied, or came from the tail. Juice on the board means it had no rest; chewy edges mean silverskin left on.

At Brennan's the Roasted Chateaubriand is on the dinner menu: Creekstone Farms beef tenderloin, roasted whole, with roasted and glazed summer squash and sauce Foyot, printed to serve two. Creekstone Farms is a Black Angus producer in Arkansas City, Kansas; never call this tenderloin Prime unless the kitchen confirms it.

The squash are young summer kinds, such as courgette, yellow squash and pattypan, roasted until their edges brown and glossed with a glaze, usually butter with a little stock or honey: a light, seasonal partner that changes with the market. Whether the roast is carved at the table or in the kitchen, and tonight's cooking time, are lineup questions.

Offer it early, to a couple celebrating or two guests who both want beef, because a whole roast takes longer than a steak; confirm the timing with the kitchen and tell the table honestly. Say plainly that it serves two, ask the temperature once and write it on the ticket. Describe it simply: the centre of the tenderloin, very tender and mild, roasted whole, with béarnaise made richer with a reduced beef glaze. The house guide suggests a shared side, Maggie's Mushrooms or the Shells & Cheese; questions about the sauce go to the kitchen.

faults.cause: Foyot spooned on to a scorching plate or left waiting under heat.

brennans.how: The Roasted Chateaubriand is Creekstone Farms tenderloin, the thick centre cut, roasted whole for two with roasted and glazed summer squash and sauce Foyot, béarnaise deepened with meat glaze to give the mild, lean cut its savour. Carving and timing are confirmed at lineup.

cards.front: What is a Chateaubriand?
cards.back: The thick centre of the beef tenderloin, cut thick and roasted whole for two, then rested and carved into round slices. Say shah-toh-bree-AHN.

cards.front: Why does a Chateaubriand want a rich sauce such as Foyot?
cards.back: Tenderloin is the tenderest cut but also the leanest and mildest, so a savoury, buttery sauce brings the depth the meat lacks.

cards.front: What is sauce Foyot?
cards.back: Béarnaise with glace de viande, a reduced meat glaze, whisked in: tawny, deeper and more savoury than plain béarnaise. Say fwah-YO.

cards.front: Whom does the name Chateaubriand honour?
cards.back: François-René de Chateaubriand, the French writer and diplomat; the story credits his chef, Montmireil, around 1822.

cards.front: Why might two butchers mean different things by chateaubriand?
cards.back: France cuts a thick steak from the heart of the fillet, some older books use the head end, and America often means the whole centre-cut roast.

cards.front: Why is a centre-cut tenderloin tied before roasting?
cards.back: String every 2.5 cm (1 inch) holds an even round, so the roast cooks evenly from end to end.

cards.front: At what centre temperature does a Chateaubriand leave the oven for medium rare?
cards.back: About 51°C (124°F); carryover heat during the rest lifts it to about 55°C (131°F).

cards.front: How is the roast rested and carved?
cards.back: Rested about 10 minutes, string removed, then carved across the grain into slices about 2 cm (3/4 inch) thick.

cards.front: How is doneness agreed for a Chateaubriand for two?
cards.back: Once, with both guests, because one roast comes to one temperature. Splitting ends and centre between them is the kitchen's call.

cards.front: What is the side on the Roasted Chateaubriand?
cards.back: Roasted and glazed summer squash: young, tender squash browned in the oven and glossed, a light seasonal partner that changes with the market.

cards.front: What must a server confirm at lineup about the Chateaubriand?
cards.back: Whether it is carved at the table or in the kitchen, tonight's cooking time, and whether the tenderloin is Prime before ever saying so.

questions.q: Which part of the beef is a Chateaubriand?
questions.answer: The thick centre of the tenderloin
distractors: The thin tail of the tenderloin
A boned rib from the forequarter
questions.why: The centre is the even, round stretch of the tenderloin, so it roasts evenly whole and carves into neat slices for two.

questions.q: Why does the Chateaubriand come with a rich, savoury sauce like Foyot?
questions.answer: Tenderloin is tender but lean and mild
distractors: Tenderloin is tough and needs softening
The sauce hides an overcooked roast
Tenderloin is too salty on its own
questions.why: The cut barely works and carries little fat, so it is tender but mild; the meat glaze and butter in Foyot supply the depth.

questions.q: What turns a béarnaise into sauce Foyot?
questions.answer: Glace de viande, meat glaze
distractors: Tomato cooked down to a paste
questions.why: Foyot is béarnaise with meat glaze; tomato makes Choron, whipped cream makes mousseline, and blood orange makes maltaise.

questions.q: Whom does the name Chateaubriand honour?
questions.answer: A French writer and diplomat
distractors: A Paris restaurant opposite the Senate
questions.why: It honours François-René de Chateaubriand; the restaurant opposite the Senate is where the name Foyot comes from.

questions.q: For a medium-rare finish, at roughly what centre temperature does the roast leave the oven?
questions.answer: About 51°C (124°F)
questions.why: Carryover heat lifts the centre to about 55°C (131°F) during the rest; pulling it at the finished temperature overshoots.

questions.q: How is a Chateaubriand carved after its rest?
questions.answer: Across the grain, about 2 cm (3/4 inch) thick
distractors: Along the grain, in long, thin strips like a fillet
Into cubes, straight from the oven
questions.why: Tenderloin fibres run the length of the muscle, so slices across them are short-fibred and tender, and the rest keeps the juice in.

questions.q: Two guests share a Chateaubriand. How is the doneness agreed?
questions.answer: Once, as one roast has one temperature
distractors: Separately, and the kitchen roasts two halves
Always well done, to suit everyone
questions.why: A whole roast comes to one temperature; any split between ends and centre is a request the kitchen decides, not a promise.

questions.q: Which detail of the Chateaubriand is a lineup question rather than something to say from memory?
questions.answer: Whether it is carved at the table
distractors: That it comes with summer squash
questions.why: The menu prints the two guests, the Foyot and the squash; whether the roast is carved at the table or in the kitchen is confirmed at lineup.

entries.title: The hanger steak with béarnaise
entries.summary: Brennan's breakfast steak and eggs: a Creole-spiced Creekstone Prime hanger, cooked hot and fast, sliced across the grain and served with French béarnaise, a smoked potato pavé and a sunny-side-up egg. The same cut returns at dinner on different foundations.
entries.guest: Our Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak is Creekstone Prime hanger with a smoked potato pavé, a sunny-side-up Vital Farms egg and classic French béarnaise. How would you like it cooked?

paras: The hanger is the butcher's steak. It hangs from the diaphragm, the sheet of muscle under the ribs that works with every breath, close to the kidneys. There is only one on each animal, so butchers often kept it for themselves, and in France it is the onglet of the bistro. A tough sinew runs down its middle and is cut out, leaving two long lobes with a loose, coarse grain. It tastes deeply beefy, with a rich, mineral edge, and it rewards hot, fast cooking.

On this plate two traditions meet. Béarnaise (bair-NAYZ), hollandaise built on a reduction of vinegar, shallot and tarragon, is the classic French sauce for beef: its sharpness cuts the richness and its herbs lift the meat. Creole spice seasons the steak itself: a blend usually built on paprika, cayenne and black pepper, though the house's own blend is not printed, so spice questions go to the kitchen. A French plate with a New Orleans accent.

Trim any membrane left on the outside and check the central sinew is gone; a whole hanger is usually split into its two lobes, each about 4 cm (1 1/2 inches) thick. Season it well with salt and the Creole spice. Sear it in a very hot pan or on a hot grill, turning it every minute or so, for about 8 to 12 minutes in all, until the crust is deep brown; for medium rare, pull it at about 52 to 54°C (126 to 129°F), and it climbs a little as it rests.

Rest it for 5 minutes, then slice it across the grain. The hanger's fibres are long and slant across each lobe, so look before you cut and turn the knife until it crosses them. Slices about 1 cm (3/8 inch) thick, cut on a slight angle, eat tenderly; cut along the grain and the same steak chews like string. Add the béarnaise last, on warm meat, never straight from a scorching pan.

The hanger is tender only while it is pink. Its coarse fibres are bundled in sheaths of connective tissue. As the meat passes about 60°C (140°F), the fibre proteins tighten and squeeze out their juice, and the collagen in the sheaths shrinks and pulls the bundles tighter still. A hanger then turns dry and stringy, and its rich flavour turns to liver. Most kitchens recommend medium rare to medium and treat medium as the limit, and the choice stays with the guest.
Other faults are simpler: a pale crust means a wet steak or a pan not hot enough, a gristly bite is the sinew left in, and juice flooding the plate means it had no rest.

The same cut stands on different foundations at dinner. The Creole Hanger Steak carries housemade Creole spice with chilli crisp, a crunchy Chinese chilli oil with real heat, a pepita persillade and Madeira-glazed broccolini, and no egg and no béarnaise. The breakfast plate leans French, sauce and potato; the dinner plate leans on heat and crunch. The dinner plate's persillade and its build belong to The menu read by method.

At Brennan's the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak is a breakfast and lunch main course: Creekstone Farms Prime hanger, a smoked potato pavé, a sunny-side-up Vital Farms egg and French béarnaise. The pavé (pah-VAY) is potato sliced paper thin, layered with cream and butter, baked, pressed overnight, cut into bricks and seared crisp; how the smoke gets in is the kitchen's detail. Vital Farms eggs are pasture raised, each hen with at least 10 square metres (108 square feet) of rotated pasture. The house guide puts the hanger at its best medium rare to medium; the menu prints both supplier names, and lineup, the short staff meeting before each service, confirms they are still current before you say them.

Take the temperature as you take the order and write it on the ticket. If a guest is unsure, say the hanger is most tender pink, but the choice is theirs. Say it plainly: steak and eggs done properly, a beefy butcher's cut with Creole spice, crisp layered potato, a runny yolk and the classic steak sauce. Keep the two hangers apart: breakfast has béarnaise and an egg, dinner has chilli crisp and neither. Questions about what is in the spice or the sauce go to the kitchen.

The dinner Creole Hanger Steak puts the same cut on other foundations: housemade Creole spice, chilli crisp, a pepita persillade and Madeira-glazed broccolini, with no egg or béarnaise. Never mix the two plates up.

entries.title: New Orleans Shrimp & Grits
entries.say: As it reads: New Orleans Shrimp & Grits.
entries.summary: Brennan's Creole answer to a Lowcountry breakfast: Louisiana shrimp in a tomato Creole sauce seasoned with tasso, over a fried pimento cheese grit cake, with fried okra chips. Creamy and crisp, smoky and tangy, built on the trinity.
entries.guest: Our Shrimp & Grits puts Louisiana shrimp in a Creole sauce with tasso over a fried pimento cheese grit cake, crisp outside and creamy inside, with crunchy okra chips.

paras: Shrimp and grits is a Southern coastal breakfast; Brennan's plate is its New Orleans version. Louisiana shrimp are cooked in Creole sauce, the city's tomato sauce built on the trinity, with tasso (TAH-so), a spiced, smoked pork, cooked into it. Under them is not a bowl of soft grits but a grit cake: grits made with pimento cheese, set firm, cut and fried until crisp outside and creamy within. Fried okra chips go on top for crunch. Learn it by its contrasts: creamy and crisp, smoky and tangy.

The dish began in the South Carolina Lowcountry, the coast around Charleston, as breakfast shrimp: fresh shrimp cooked in butter or bacon fat and eaten over grits. Charleston recipes for it were in print by 1930. In 1985 Craig Claiborne wrote up Bill Neal's version from Crook's Corner in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, with bacon, lemon and cheese grits, in The New York Times, and it went national.

The old Charleston recipes dress the shrimp in butter; Bill Neal's Chapel Hill version uses bacon fat and lemon. The New Orleans plate swaps both for a tomato Creole sauce on the trinity, with tasso for smoke.

Grits are coarse-ground dried corn. The old Southern name is hominy grits, and some are still ground from hominy, corn soaked in an alkali to loosen its hull; stone-ground grits keep more of the germ and take longer. For a cake, simmer about 1 part grits to 4 or 5 parts water, milk or stock by volume, stirring often, until thick and tender: about 5 minutes for quick grits, 40 to 60 minutes for stone-ground. Fold in the cheese off the heat, spread the grits 2 cm (3/4 inch) deep in a lined tray and chill until firm, at least 2 hours.

Cut the set grits into cakes, dust them in flour or cornmeal and fry them at 175 to 185°C (347 to 365°F) until golden, 2 to 3 minutes a side in a shallow pan. Drain them on a rack and salt them at once. The okra chips are thin slices or strips of okra, dusted and fried in the same hot oil: cooked fast, okra turns crisp and nutty before it can turn slippery.

The Creole sauce begins with the trinity, onion, celery and green pepper, softened in fat, with diced tasso browned first in a little fat so its smoke and spice flavour the pan; tomato, stock and herbs then simmer into a coating sauce. Creole sauce, Tasso and Okra each have their own entry. The shrimp go in last, for 2 to 3 minutes, just until pink and curled into a loose C. A tight O means overcooked and rubbery.

A cake that falls apart was cooked too loose or chilled too briefly; a greasy one met oil that was too cool, often from crowding the pan. Rubbery shrimp cooked too long, slimy okra was cut thick or fried slowly, and a soggy cake sat under its sauce too long: fry the cake to order and spoon the shrimp and sauce over it at the pass, the counter where the kitchen finishes plates and hands them to the servers.

At Brennan's the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits is a breakfast and lunch main course: Louisiana shrimp, a fried pimento cheese grit cake, tasso, Creole sauce and fried okra chips. Pimento cheese is grated sharp cheddar bound with mayonnaise and sweet red pimientos; folded into the grits before they set, it makes the cake tangy and creamy inside. Louisiana is one of the country's largest shrimp producers, so the word on the menu is worth saying. Whether the tasso is smoked in house, and whether tonight's shrimp are brown or white, are questions for the kitchen. The house guide gives TAH-so; TASS-oh is also heard, and the house habit is a question for lineup, the short staff meeting before each service.

Tell the guest it comes as a fried cake, so nobody expects a creamy bowl. Describe it the house way: creamy and crisp, smoky and tangy, with mild to moderate spice from the tasso and the sauce. It suits a guest who wants something savoury and Southern, or someone trying grits for the first time. When a guest asks about shellfish, pork, cheese or fried coatings, read the service note and take the question to the kitchen.

brennans.how: Louisiana shrimp in a tomato Creole sauce with tasso, over grits made with pimento cheese, set, cut and fried into a cake, with fried okra chips: the Lowcountry breakfast made Creole, a tomato sauce on the trinity in place of the Carolina butter or bacon and lemon gravy.

cards.front: What is on Brennan's New Orleans Shrimp & Grits?
cards.back: Louisiana shrimp in Creole sauce with tasso (TAH-so), a spiced smoked pork, over a fried pimento cheese grit cake, topped with fried okra chips.

cards.front: How does the Lowcountry dish differ from the New Orleans one?
cards.back: The Carolina dish sits in butter, or in Neal's bacon and lemon pan gravy, over soft grits; ours sits in a tomato Creole sauce with tasso over a fried grit cake.

cards.front: Where did shrimp and grits begin, and what made it famous?
cards.back: As a Lowcountry breakfast around Charleston, printed by 1930; Bill Neal's version at Crook's Corner, written up by Craig Claiborne in 1985, carried it across the country.

cards.front: What exactly are grits made from?
cards.back: Coarse-ground dried corn, the hominy grits of the old South, simmered slowly in liquid until thick and creamy.

cards.front: What ratio of grits to liquid sets a firm cake?
cards.back: About 1 part grits to 4 or 5 parts liquid by volume, cooked thick, spread 2 cm (3/4 inch) deep and chilled until firm.

cards.front: How is the grit cake fried crisp rather than greasy?
cards.back: Dusted and fried at 175 to 185°C (347 to 365°F) until golden, in small batches, then drained on a rack and salted at once.

cards.front: What foundation does the Creole sauce start from?
cards.back: The holy trinity, onion, celery and green pepper, softened in fat, with tasso browned first for smoke and spice, then tomato and stock.

cards.front: How do you know shrimp are cooked and not overcooked?
cards.back: They turn pink and curl into a loose C in 2 to 3 minutes; a tight O means they have gone rubbery.

cards.front: Why are the okra chips fried fast in hot oil?
cards.back: Quick, hot frying turns okra crisp and nutty before its slippery juices can come out.

cards.front: What is pimento cheese, and what does it do in the cake?
cards.back: Sharp cheddar, mayonnaise and sweet red pimientos; folded into the grits, it makes the fried cake tangy and creamy inside.

cards.front: How does a server describe the Shrimp & Grits?
cards.back: Creamy and crisp, smoky and tangy, with mild to moderate spice, and the grits come as a fried cake, not a bowl.

questions.q: What sets the New Orleans shrimp and grits apart from the Charleston dish?
questions.answer: A tomato Creole sauce with tasso
distractors: A bacon and lemon pan gravy
A cream sauce with white wine
A brown gravy on a dark roux
questions.why: The Carolina plates use butter or a bacon and lemon pan gravy; the New Orleans plate carries a tomato Creole sauce on the trinity, smoky with tasso.

questions.q: Where did shrimp and grits begin?
questions.answer: The Carolina Lowcountry
questions.why: It began as breakfast shrimp on the coast around Charleston, with a Charleston recipe in print by 1930.

questions.q: What are the grits on the plate made from?
questions.answer: Coarse-ground dried corn
questions.why: Grits are dried corn ground coarse, the old hominy grits of the South, simmered slowly until thick and creamy.

questions.q: Roughly how much liquid do grits need, by volume, to set a firm cake?
questions.answer: 4 to 5 parts liquid to 1 of grits
questions.why: Four to five parts liquid cooks the grits tender and thick enough to set firm when chilled; much more and the cake will not hold.

questions.q: What shape tells you a shrimp is cooked but not overcooked?
questions.answer: A loose C
questions.why: Shrimp curl as they cook; a loose C in 2 to 3 minutes is done, and a tight O has gone rubbery.

questions.q: Why is okra for chips fried quickly in hot oil?
questions.answer: So it crisps before it turns slippery
distractors: So it soaks up more of the frying oil
So it stays raw in the middle
questions.why: Fast, hot frying sets a crisp, nutty surface before the slippery juices inside the pod can come out.

questions.q: At what oil temperature are the grit cakes fried?
questions.why: That heat browns the coating fast while the inside warms through; cooler oil soaks in and hotter oil burns the crust.

questions.q: What should a server tell a guest before they order the Shrimp & Grits?
questions.answer: That the grits come as a fried cake
distractors: That the grits come as a soft bowl
That the sauce is a bacon and lemon gravy
That the okra is stewed until silky
questions.why: Many guests expect a creamy bowl; saying it comes as a crisp fried cake, creamy inside, sets the right picture.

entries.title: Bananas Foster at the table
entries.say: As it reads: Bananas Foster at the table.
entries.summary: Brennan's signature dessert, created in 1951 and flamed at the guéridon: bananas in butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, banana liqueur and burning rum, spooned over housemade vanilla ice cream. The story, the service and the words to say.
entries.guest: Bananas Foster was created at Brennan's in 1951. We cook bananas in butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, flame them with rum at your table and spoon them over our vanilla ice cream.

paras: Bananas Foster is the dessert Brennan's gave the world, and here it is made in front of the guest. On a guéridon (gay-ree-DOHN), the tableside cart, butter, brown sugar and cinnamon melt into a caramel, the bananas soften in it, rum is set alight, and all of it is spooned over housemade vanilla ice cream, hot over cold. It is cooked in one pan for at least two, which is why it is ordered in twos. The house calls it the most ordered dish on the menu; whether to say so at the table is a question for lineup, the short staff meeting before each service.

It was created in 1951, while the restaurant was still Owen Brennan's Vieux Carré on Bourbon Street, five years before the move to 417 Royal Street. Owen asked for a new dessert for a dinner honouring his friend Richard Foster of the New Orleans Crime Commission. His sister Ella Brennan and the chef Paul Blangé (blahn-ZHAY) adapted a family dish, the caramelised bananas their mother made at home, and named it for Foster.

That is the telling on the house's own Traditions and recipe pages; the server guide tells it as Owen's challenge to Blangé. Which telling to use, and which name for the commission (it is also called the Metropolitan Crime Commission), are a manager's call at lineup.
Bananas made sense. New Orleans was then the great port of entry for bananas from Central and South America. 2026 is the dessert's 75th year.

The kitchen build belongs to Bananas Foster; at the table, learn the order, because the guest watches every step. The cart is set where nothing hangs overhead, with the spirits measured into small vessels beforehand.

Butter and brown sugar melt and bubble into a smooth, blond caramel, dusted with cinnamon. Banana liqueur goes in, as the house's published recipe has it. The bananas, ripe but firm, halved and quartered, are laid in and turned once so they soften without collapsing. The pan comes off the flame, the measured rum goes in, and back on the flame the pan is tilted so the far edge catches, away from the guests. As it burns, the caramel deepens; when the flame has died, the bananas go over the ice cream and the warm sauce follows.

The menu prints rum; the published recipe adds banana liqueur. Follow the cart build confirmed at lineup, and never quote quantities. The flame rules belong to Flambé safety, learned word for word; a new server never lights a pan before sign off.

Bananas that collapse were too ripe or stewed too long. A sauce that sets hard on the ice cream was taken past blond into toffee. Ice cream melted to soup was scooped too early. In a bright room the flame can be almost invisible, so treat the pan as lit until it has clearly died. A guest leaning in is too close: seat everyone back before the rum goes in.

World Famous Bananas Foster is printed at breakfast, lunch and dinner, and it closes the Traditional Breakfast tasting, with Congregation Coffee & Chicory. The menu prints it flambéed tableside, with a minimum of two per order; whether the printed price is per person or per order is a lineup question, so never quote it until a manager says. The ice cream is made in house, and questions about what goes into it go to the kitchen. Who performs the flambé is a question for the manager.

Seed it with the main course order, so the cart is ready when the table is: every first visit, every celebration, every guest who asks what Brennan's is famous for. Remind the table it is made for two or more. Pour any wine before the flambé starts, so no glass sits near the flame.

Tell the story while the caramel bubbles: created at Brennan's in 1951, named for Richard Foster. Then the cue, "Now the rum, please sit back just a little", and stop talking. Let the flame have the room. When it has died, one line as you plate: over our vanilla ice cream, then the warm sauce.

Be exact about alcohol: flaming burns the vapour above the pan, and much of the alcohol stays in the sauce. Tell any guest who avoids alcohol before they order, and steer them to the Lemon Tart or the Pineapple Tarte Tatin.

faults.cause: Fruit too ripe, or left too long in the caramel.
faults.fix: Choose ripe but firm bananas and turn them once, just until they soften.

faults.fault: The sauce sets hard on the ice cream
faults.cause: The caramel was taken past blond towards toffee.
faults.fix: Keep the caramel blond and bubbling before the liqueur goes in.

faults.fault: Ice cream melted before the sauce arrives
faults.cause: Scooped at the start of the service.
faults.fix: Scoop as the flame dies, so cold meets hot at the last moment.

faults.cause: A bright room hides the burning vapour.
faults.fix: Treat the pan as lit until the flame has clearly died, and keep guests back.

components: Bananas, butter, brown sugar and cinnamon
brennans.how: Created in 1951 for Owen Brennan's friend Richard Foster, it is made at the guéridon: butter, brown sugar and cinnamon to a caramel, banana liqueur, the bananas, then rum, lit under the house's seven safety steps, all spooned over housemade vanilla ice cream, two or more to an order.

sources.title: The legend of Bananas Foster, a Brennan's New Orleans original, New Orleans & Company

cards.front: When and where was Bananas Foster created?
cards.back: In 1951, at Brennan's while it was still Owen Brennan's Vieux Carré on Bourbon Street, five years before the move to Royal Street.

cards.front: Who is Bananas Foster named for?
cards.back: Richard Foster, Owen Brennan's friend, of the New Orleans Crime Commission (also called the Metropolitan Crime Commission), honoured at a dinner in 1951; which name to use is a lineup question.

cards.front: Who created Bananas Foster, and how is the story told?
cards.back: Chef Paul Blangé, in 1951, at Owen Brennan's request; the house's own pages credit Ella Brennan with him. Whether to tell it as Owen's challenge to Blangé or as Ella and Blangé adapting their mother's caramelised bananas is confirmed with a manager.

cards.front: Why a banana dessert, in New Orleans in 1951?
cards.back: New Orleans was the great port of entry for bananas from Central and South America, so the fruit was close at hand.

cards.front: In what order does the pan build at the guéridon?
cards.back: Butter, brown sugar and cinnamon to a blond caramel; banana liqueur; the bananas, turned once; then rum, added off the flame and lit.

cards.front: What is a guéridon?
cards.back: The tableside cart, said gay-ree-DOHN, on which the Foster is cooked and flamed in front of the guests.

cards.front: Why is Bananas Foster ordered in twos?
cards.back: It is cooked in one pan at the table for at least two people, so the menu prints a minimum of two per order; a guest dining alone is a question for the manager.

cards.front: When does the server stop talking during the Foster?
cards.back: As the rum goes in: give the cue to sit back a little, then let the flame have the room, and speak again as you plate.

cards.front: Does the flame burn off all the alcohol?
cards.back: No. Flaming burns the vapour above the pan; much of the alcohol stays in the sauce, so tell any guest who avoids it.

cards.front: Who may light the Foster pan at Brennan's?
cards.back: Only staff signed off on the house procedure; a new server never lights a pan before sign off, and who flames is a lineup question.

cards.front: When should a server first mention Bananas Foster?
cards.back: With the main course order, so the cart can be ready: every first visit, every celebration, every guest asking what the house is famous for.

questions.q: In what year was Bananas Foster created at Brennan's?
questions.why: It was created in 1951 on Bourbon Street; 1946 is the founding, 1956 the move to Royal Street and 2014 the reopening.

questions.q: Richard Foster, for whom the dessert is named, was a member of what?
questions.answer: The New Orleans Crime Commission
distractors: The Board of the Port of New Orleans
A Central American fruit company's board
questions.why: Foster was Owen Brennan's friend and a figure of the city's crime commission; the house pages print New Orleans Crime Commission, and which name to use at the table is a lineup question.

questions.q: Why was a banana dessert a natural choice in New Orleans in 1951?
questions.answer: The city was the great port of entry for bananas
distractors: Bananas grew in the Brennan's courtyard
Louisiana farms grew most of the nation's bananas
A banana festival was held that week
questions.why: Bananas from Central and South America came into the country through New Orleans, so the fruit was close at hand.

questions.q: In the house's published recipe, what goes into the caramel just before the rum is added?
questions.answer: The bananas
questions.why: Butter, sugar and cinnamon make the caramel, banana liqueur loosens it, the bananas soften in it, and only then is the rum added and lit.

questions.q: When should the server stop talking during the Foster service?
questions.answer: As the rum goes in and the flame rises
distractors: As the bananas are laid in
Only once the plates are cleared from the table
questions.why: The story comes while the caramel bubbles; at the rum the server gives the cue to sit back, then lets the flame have the room.

questions.q: A guest asks whether the flame burns off all the alcohol. What is the accurate answer?
questions.answer: No, much of it stays in the sauce
distractors: Yes, if the flame lasts ten seconds
Only the liqueur stays, not the rum
questions.why: The flame burns the vapour above the pan, not all the alcohol in it, so guests who avoid alcohol are told before they order.

questions.q: Why does Bananas Foster carry a minimum of two per order?
questions.answer: It is cooked in one pan for at least two
distractors: It is only served at large tables
The rum is sold by the pair of glasses
questions.why: The Foster is made in one pan at the table for at least two people, so the menu prints a minimum of two; a solo guest's request goes to the manager.

questions.q: Who may light the Bananas Foster pan at Brennan's?
questions.answer: Only staff signed off on the procedure
distractors: Any server who has watched it done
Any server free when the order fires
The guest, if they ask to try
questions.why: Staff train before they flame at the table; a new server never lights a pan before sign off, and who flames is confirmed with the manager.
